title: Design Product-Feed Recommendations
prompt:
Design a recommendation system for a product feed.

Clarify what the feed contains, who uses it, and what a successful recommendation means. Explain the data, model, serving path and evaluation, with the assumptions you need to make.

**Related interview variant:** suppose the product is an Amazon-style shopping experience. How would your design differ between recommendations on the landing page and recommendations within a search experience?

The reports do not prescribe a catalog size, label, latency target or model family. State your working assumptions and explain which design decisions would change if they were wrong. A written ML system design is expected.
background_note: Two original MLE reports describe a product-feed recommender and an Amazon-style recommender with landing-page versus search contexts. The latter is presented as a separate reported variant, not a follow-up proven to have occurred in the former interview. Product details, labels, model architecture and serving assumptions in the answer are illustrative. Generic Jira-recommender mentions with unknown targets were not promoted to this contract.

response.placeholder: Start with clarifying questions and state your assumptions. Then describe your design, evaluation, failure handling and trade-offs.
response.reference_answer:
## Define the recommendation unit

Ask what an item is, how the feed is used and which outcome matters. For a working shopping example, choose useful product discovery that can lead to satisfactory purchases, with negative feedback, returns and latency as guardrails. A click objective alone can reward misleading suggestions. Clarify eligibility, available inventory and whether repeat exposure is acceptable.

## Data and training

Log impressions, positions, eligible candidates, interactions and mature outcomes with user/session context, item state and model versions. Build point-in-time features; a future purchase or current inventory snapshot must not leak into a past training example. Delayed purchase/return labels need a maturity window. Distinguish not-shown items from shown-but-ignored items and discuss controlled exploration or debiasing before treating implicit feedback as unbiased truth.

## Retrieval and ranking

Retrieve candidates from behavior-based, content-based and fresh/popular sources. A two-tower model can help at large scale, but a smaller catalog may not justify it. Measure candidate recall before optimizing the ranker. Score with user, item and session features; combine relevance and expected utility, then apply eligibility, diversity and repetition policies. Treat cold users and new products explicitly, using available context and content rather than fabricating behavior.

## Home versus search

A landing page has no explicit query, so longer-term preference, recent session behavior and exploration matter. Search has an immediate query intent: lexical/semantic match and hard query constraints should bound personalization. A highly clickable unrelated item is still a poor search result. Keep query-conditioned retrieval, relevance labels and evaluation slices separate from the queryless feed.

## Serving and evaluation

Use bounded retrieval and ranking stages with fresh eligibility checks. Cache carefully around inventory and user context; fall back to eligible popular or lexical results when personalization fails. Offline metrics include retrieval recall, ranking quality and calibration. Online experiments measure discovery/purchase success with return rates, repetition, diversity, latency and longer-term satisfaction. Inspect new-user, new-item and infrequent-category slices. Monitor feature freshness, exposure concentration and delayed outcome drift, and retain independent rollback for retrieval and ranking.
